articles.title: Living with tinnitus can be distressing. So what can you do about it?
articles.summary: Tinnitus affects millions of people and it can take many different forms. But there are therapies that can help make it more bearable. For some it’s a high-pitched mosquito whine; for others it’s a low bass hum.
body: Whatever form it takes, tinnitus – hearing sounds like ringing, buzzing or hissing when no external noise is there – can be extremely distressing because it’s quite literally in your head; there is no escaping it. Given that at least one-quarter of the population report experiencing tinnitus at some stage in their life, it’s surprising how little is understood about why.

“The theory that’s most supported at the moment is that there’s some sort of change in the hearing pathway, and the nerves in the hearing pathway are basically firing more than they should do,” says Dr Emma Laird, an audiologist at La Trobe University in Melbourne. “We’re hearing this increased activity as that tinnitus sound.”

There is no cure for tinnitus but the good news is that there is a variety of treatment approaches – audiological, psychological, physiotherapeutic and technological – that can be effective at helping people to manage the condition. “I’ve had tinnitus for probably 20 years now,” Laird says. “Because I’ve habituated to it – so my brain can just pop it at the back of my head – it’s not causing distress day to day.”
points: Tinnitus affects millions of people and it can take many different forms.
But there are therapies that can help make it more bearable.
For some it’s a high-pitched mosquito whine; for others it’s a low bass hum.
“I’ve had tinnitus for probably 20 years now,” Laird says.
articles.author: Bianca Nogrady

articles.title: I'm a pro chef – here's why this tiny knife sharpener belongs in the kitchen of any serious cook
articles.summary: This sharpener is easy to use and does the job well enough to please a professional chef. The seven best air fryers, tried and tested in a food lab. Sign up for the Filter US newsletter, your weekly guide to buying fewer, better things.
body: I n every cooking class that I teach, knife sharpening is the first lesson my students learn. Dull knives are inefficient and dangerous – a dull blade can slide right off the curvature of an onion into the flesh of the hand holding it.

At the Drexel Food Lab, where I’m a certified research chef and culinary educator, we use a Tormek T2 Pro Kitchen Knife Sharpener, donated by the company, to sharpen our knives. It is a dream piece of equipment that can sharpen any knife we throw at it, from a pile of our classes’ cheap stainless steel Dexter kitchen knives to a high-end carbon steel Japanese slicer for our instructors’ use.

But at nearly $900 and 14lbs, the T2 is overkill if you’re not running a professional kitchen. It’s driving a Lamborghini in stop-and-go city traffic. For easy home use, I recommend the Horl 3, a simple-to-learn rolling knife sharpener with a stand that holds the knife in place at the optimal angle. Co-founder Otmar Horl, an engineer, together with his son, Timo, a graphic designer and barbecue enthusiast, designed the first rolling knife sharpening system that became the Horl 3 in the basement of their family home, where they produced the first 200 units by hand.
points: This sharpener is easy to use and does the job well enough to please a professional chef.

articles.title: Shared memories of losing a parent | Letters
articles.summary: Gaby Hinsliff’s moving piece about the death of her mother brought back memories for Bob Dawson, John Lovell and Patrick Thomas. Gosh, what a moving article by Gaby Hinsliff ( Losing a parent is a bewildering, lonely experience. Here are the things I wish I had known before, 5 September ).
body: I thought Gaby Hinsliff’s piece on losing a parent was beautifully done. It reminded me of my mother’s sudden death in 2010. We were inundated with sympathy cards. I’d not realised their importance before. Each one gave us a multitude of insights into Mum’s life and her interaction with others. Indeed, I felt I only got a true picture of her in death through the countless stories of small acts of kindness and selflessness.

articles.title: The 12 Essential Kitchen Tools for Beginners, According to Cooking Instructors
articles.summary: Every time I see a meat tenderizer, I think of my mother. Specifically of the way in which she, as someone wary of emotional vulnerability yet full of affection (classic Boomer combo), decided to make Austrian pork schnitzel her love language — and the meat tenderizer her translator.
body: That tenderizer has become a staple of my kitchen ecosystem today. But one person’s tenderizer is another’s hand-me-down whisk, Japanese chef’s knife, or grill press. So what do other people consider their ride-or-die cooking tools? What are the baseline peelers, knives, and spatulas that are in constant rotation, the tools that make you feel like a culinary John Wick? I decided to ask not just chefs, but chefs with culinary school teaching experience (aka endless patience and a knowledge of novice-level skillsets) about what they consider to be the best beginner cooking tools.

In addition to a few of my own cooking essentials, I picked the brains of four teachers with experience in a variety of programs, from Hot Bread Kitchen — a New York City nonprofit that helps immigrants break into the food industry — to the legendary Institute of Culinary Education, all in the hopes of answering the inherently relative question of what constitutes an essential cooking tool for beginners.
Don’t: Spend more than you need to on, say, a pair of tongs. And if you’re lucky enough to have a grandpa with a sick filet knife, maybe ask him about it.

articles.title: Moncler Cut the Ribbon on its New Manhattan Flagship with Help From Some Very Famous Friends
articles.summary: Cher, Julia Roberts, Jessica Chastain, and Anne Hathaway joined Moncler as it opened the doors to its new 23,680-square-foot flagship on Fifth Avenue—making it officially the brand’s largest store in the world.
body: Between the A-list faces, who showed up in the brand from head-to-toe, and a crowd of hundreds, the ribbon cutting was perhaps the liveliest Flatiron District retail store opening ever. Despite the 86-degree, balmy September day, the Monclers were out in force, too. A few brave folk donned classic down jackets, like Jordan Clarkson in a custom one-of-one Knicks-appointed blue and orange bomber. Meanwhile Serena Williams opted for a white padded skirt, Olivia Palermo layered a lightweight shacket, and Future opted for a technical tracksuit.

Friends of the brand reminisced on their favorite Moncler moments. Cher, whose arrival garnered shrieks of excitement and eager whispers from Jessica Chastain. “I have a Moncler that I love especially. I got it in Monte Carlo, and it’s a little vest and it was sparkly—so of course I was drawn to it,” Cher told Vogue.

articles.summary: It helped that it was set to be the very first event thrown at Straker’s—Thomas Straker’s first permanent digs in the city—in the former Lucky Strike space on SoHo’s Grand Street.
body: Incredible women: New York Fashion Week certainly has no shortage of them. And in between a marathon of shows taking place across the city, many of them—stylists, editors, and models at the top of their game—took the chance to take a load off their stiletto-clad feet and stop by Net-a-Porter’s very popular party.

Out front, almost concealed from street view by a black Net-a-Porter delivery van, flashbulbs were popping as Serena Williams, in a regal purple Loewe number, posed against the exterior of the restaurant. Just inside the door, a Tom Ford-clad Emmy Rossum was keeping a social media editor happy by obliging in a tiny mic interview. Katie Holmes and her boyfriend Jason Bard Yarmosky were among those who peeped into the kitchen to see Straker—who found viral fame a few years back with his butter videos on social media—doing his thing.

articles.title: A Mega Guest List Came Together For a Major Cause at Kering’s Caring for Women Dinner
articles.summary: This year, Kering Foundation co-founders Salma Hayek Pinault and François-Henri Pinault co-hosted the evening alongside Pamela Anderson, Simone Biles, Benicio Del Toro, Nacho Figueras, Dakota Johnson, and Lorna Simpson.
body: It is the house of Kering, after all, so the evening called for a black tie dress code, and no one seemed interested in underdressing. Guests used the occasion to turn out in the glitzy Gucci (Paris Hilton; Alix Earle), leather-forward Balenciaga (Biles; Jordan Roth), and slinky Valentino (Johnson; Colman Domingo). Conversation drifted from the shows and spectacles of the week, to the true raison d’être of the night: championing women through crisis.

“Supporting women is a lifelong feat and effort that I will be working on for the rest of my career,” actress Camila Morrone told Vogue. “It just makes so much sense that Salma is behind it all because she’s been such a champion of women from the start.”

Paris Hilton agreed. “I love Salma. She’s so beautiful inside and out and has such a big heart,” she praised. “I think it’s amazing that she’s bringing together all these people to support such an amazing and really impactful cause.” Hilton added that when she was asked to DJ the evening, “it was an immediate yes.”
